name: Cable High Fly
aliases: Cable chest fly from high pulley
grip: Neutral or semi-pronated grip holding single D-handles with wrists straight.
description: Sweep dual high-cable handles downward and inward along a hugging arc toward the waist while standing in a staggered stance, isolating the lower and sternal sternocostal pectoralis fibers.
setup: Attach single D-handles to two high cable pulleys positioned at or above head height.
Grasp a handle in each hand and step forward between the towers into an athletic staggered stance.
Lean your torso forward approximately 15 to 20 degrees with a flat spine, holding arms wide at chest level with elbows softly bent.
instructions: Sweep both handles downward and forward in a wide hugging arc until your hands meet or cross slightly in front of your hips.
Maintain a fixed, soft bend in your elbows throughout the entire arc (avoid pressing or straightening into a pushdown).
Pause for a brief count at the bottom peak contraction, squeezing the lower and inner chest firmly.
Slowly allow your arms to open back out and upward along the same arc until you feel a comfortable stretch across the chest.
cues: Lead with the elbows in a wide hugging arc.
Squeeze hands down to the hips.
commonMistakes: Pressing the handles forward like a chest press instead of sweeping in an arc.
Swinging the torso backward and forward to generate momentum.
Straightening elbows into a triceps pushdown at the finish.

logging.example: Weight pins set to 15 kg on each tower: record 15 kg per cable stack.
logging.note: Dual cable stations use independent weight stacks; record the selected stack pin load per side.

variantNote: Standing high-to-low cable chest fly performed from dual high pulleys. Emphasizes sternal and costal fibers of the pectoralis major through downward horizontal adduction.
reviewNotes: Drafted from FitTrack ID 73 (Cable High Fly).

FitTrack description notes 'targets upper chest', but downward high-to-low trajectory biomechanically recruits sternocostal (lower/sternal) fibers; low-to-high recruits clavicular (upper) fibers. Documented explicitly.
